chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Semi-Supervised Learning
content:
Semi-supervised learning trains a model using a small labeled set \\
$L=\{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m)\}$ together with a much larger unlabeled set \\
$U=\{x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{m+n}\}$ whose true class $y$ is unknown. The goal is to use the pattern found in both sets together to build a better classifier than the labeled data alone could produce.

This sits exactly between the supervised setting of Chapter 2 (every example labeled) and the unsupervised setting of Chapter 3 (no example labeled).

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.1 --- Recognizing a Semi-Supervised Dataset
content:
A dataset has 100 emails: 15 are marked Spam or NotSpam by a human, and the remaining 85 have no label at all. Is this a semi-supervised learning problem?

Solution:
Labeled count $=15$, Unlabeled count $=85$. Since both a nonzero labeled set and a nonzero unlabeled set exist together in the same training data: \\
\boxed{\text{Yes, this is a semi-supervised learning problem}}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.2 --- Recognizing a Fully Supervised Dataset
content:
A dataset has 50 patient records, and every single record has a confirmed Disease/NoDisease label. Is this a semi-supervised learning problem?

Solution:
Labeled count $=50$, Unlabeled count $=0$. Since there is no unlabeled portion at all:
\boxed{\text{No, this is an ordinary (fully) supervised learning problem}}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.3 --- Recognizing an Unsupervised Dataset
content:
A dataset has 200 customer purchase records, and none of them have any class label attached. Is this a semi-supervised learning problem?

Solution:
Labeled count $=0$, Unlabeled count $=200$. Since there is no labeled portion at all to anchor the classes:
\boxed{\text{No, this is an unsupervised learning problem (clustering, Chapter 3)}}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Where Semi-Supervised Learning Fits: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Supervised
content:
Where Semi-Supervised Learning Fits:

1. Supervised (Chapter 2): $L$ only, $U=\varnothing$
2. Unsupervised (Chapter 3): $U$ only, $L=\varnothing$
3. Semi-supervised (this section): both $L\neq\varnothing$ and $U\neq\varnothing$ used together
4. Semi-supervised learning is valuable because labeling data (by a human) is expensive, while unlabeled data is often cheap and plentiful

\subsection{The Expectation-Maximization Framework}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm
content:
EM is an iterative procedure for estimating model parameters when some data is incomplete (here, the missing piece is the class label $y$ of the unlabeled examples). It alternates between two steps until the parameters stop changing:

- E-step (Expectation): using the current parameters, compute the probability of each possible class for every unlabeled example — a soft (fractional) label rather than a hard 0/1 label.
- M-step (Maximization): using the labeled data together with these fractional soft labels, recompute the parameters that best fit all the data.

This is the same "guess, then refine, then guess again" idea as k-Means (Section 3.2): k-Means alternates Assign and Update; EM alternates E-step and M-step, except EM assigns fractional membership instead of putting each point in exactly one cluster.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Properties of the EM Algorithm
content:
1. Each round of E-step followed by M-step never decreases how well the parameters fit the data \hfill(monotonic improvement)
2. EM is guaranteed to converge, but only to a local optimum, not necessarily the best possible parameters \hfill(local convergence, same caution as k-Means)
3. The E-step produces soft (fractional, e.g. 0.3/0.7) class probabilities for unlabeled points, not hard single-class labels \hfill(soft assignment)
4. The initial parameters (estimated from $L$ alone) affect where EM converges \hfill(initialization sensitivity)

\subsection{EM for Semi-Supervised Naive Bayes Classification}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: EM Algorithm for Semi-Supervised Naive Bayes
content:
Input: labeled examples $L$ with known class and attribute values, unlabeled examples $U$ with only attribute values

Output: class priors $P(C_k)$, attribute likelihoods $P(A_i\mid C_k)$, and soft labels for $U$

1. Using only $L$, estimate initial priors $P(C_k)$ and likelihoods $P(A_i\mid C_k)$ exactly as in ordinary Naive Bayes (Section 2.2).
2. E-step: for every unlabeled example $x\in U$, compute the (unnormalized) score $P(C_k)\prod_i P(A_i\mid C_k)$ for each class $C_k$, then normalize these scores to sum to $1$ — this gives the soft label $P(C_k\mid x)$.
3. M-step: recompute every prior and likelihood using both the labeled data (weight $1$ per example) and every unlabeled example (weighted by its soft label from step 2) as fractional counts.
4. If the parameters changed from the previous round, go back to step 2; otherwise stop.
5. Return the final parameters and the final soft labels for $U$.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.4 --- Initializing Parameters from Labeled Data
content:
The labeled set $L$ below records Weather and whether cricket was played.
| \toprule Weather | PlayCricket |
|---|---|
| \midrule Sunny | Yes |
| Sunny | Yes |
| Rainy | Yes |
| Rainy | No |
| Rainy | No |
| Sunny | No |
| \bottomrule |  |
Compute the initial Naive Bayes parameters $P(\text{Yes})$, $P(\text{No})$, $P(\text{Sunny}\mid\text{Yes})$, $P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes})$, $P(\text{Sunny}\mid\text{No})$, $P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No})$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Yes}) &= \frac{3}{6} = 0.5, \qquad P(\text{No}) = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Sunny}\mid\text{Yes}) &= \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.667, \qquad P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes}) = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333 \\
P(\text{Sunny}\mid\text{No}) &= \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333, \qquad P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No}) = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.667
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Initial parameters computed exactly as ordinary Naive Bayes on } L \text{ alone}}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.5 --- E-step: Soft-Labeling an Unlabeled Example
content:
An unlabeled example $U_1$ has Weather $=$ Rainy. Using the parameters from Example 4.4, compute the soft label $P(\text{Yes}\mid U_1)$ and $P(\text{No}\mid U_1)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{score}(\text{Yes}) &= P(\text{Yes})\cdot P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes}) = (0.5)(0.333) \approx 0.1667 \\
\text{score}(\text{No}) &= P(\text{No})\cdot P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No}) = (0.5)(0.667) \approx 0.3333 \\[4pt]
\text{Total} &= 0.1667+0.3333 = 0.5 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Yes}\mid U_1) &= \frac{0.1667}{0.5} \approx 0.333, \qquad P(\text{No}\mid U_1) = \frac{0.3333}{0.5} \approx 0.667
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{U_1 \text{ is soft-labeled } 33.3\%\text{ Yes and } 66.7\%\text{ No (not a hard 0/1 label)}}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Example 4.6 --- M-step: Updating Parameters with Fractional Counts
content:
Using the labeled set $L$ from Example 4.4 and the soft-labeled $U_1$ (Weather $=$ Rainy) from Example 4.5, recompute $P(\text{Yes})$, $P(\text{No})$, $P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes})$, and $P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No})$.

Solution:
$U_1$ contributes a fractional count of $0.333$ toward the Yes class and $0.667$ toward the No class.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{New Yes count} &= 3 + 0.333 = 3.333, \qquad \text{New No count} = 3 + 0.667 = 3.667 \\
\text{New total} &= 3.333+3.667 = 7 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Yes}) &= \frac{3.333}{7} \approx 0.476, \qquad P(\text{No}) = \frac{3.667}{7} \approx 0.524
\end{align*}$$
For the attribute likelihood, $U_1$'s Rainy value adds $0.333$ to the Yes-Rainy count and $0.667$ to the No-Rainy count:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{New Yes-Rainy count} &= 1+0.333 = 1.333, \qquad \text{New Yes total} = 3.333 \\
P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes}) &= \frac{1.333}{3.333} = 0.4 \\[6pt]
\text{New No-Rainy count} &= 2+0.667 = 2.667, \qquad \text{New No total} = 3.667 \\
P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No}) &= \frac{2.667}{3.667} \approx 0.727
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P(\text{Yes})\approx0.476,\ P(\text{No})\approx0.524,\ P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{Yes})=0.4,\ P(\text{Rainy}\mid\text{No})\approx0.727}
These updated parameters would now be used to redo the E-step, and the cycle repeats until the parameters stop changing (convergence).

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Why EM Helps Here: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Using
content:
Why EM Helps Here:

1. Using $L$ alone (Example 4.4) gives parameters based on only 6 examples
2. EM lets the unlabeled example $U_1$ contribute information too, proportional to how confident the model currently is about its class (Example 4.5), rather than guessing a hard label
3. After the M-step (Example 4.6), the parameters shift slightly — toward whichever class the soft label favored more (here, No shifted up because $U_1$ was $66.7\%$ likely No)
4. With a large unlabeled set $U$, this fractional-counting process can noticeably sharpen a classifier trained from only a small labeled set $L$

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Reinforcement Learning
content:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a learning setting in which an agent interacts with an environment over a sequence of time steps. At each step the agent observes the current state, chooses an action, and receives a numerical reward along with the next state. The agent learns, purely through this trial-and-error interaction, a policy (a rule for choosing actions) that maximizes the total reward it collects over time.

Unlike every algorithm in Chapters 2 and 3, RL has no fixed dataset at all — the agent generates its own training data by acting and observing the consequences.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Core RL Terminology: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Agent the
content:
Core RL Terminology:

1. Agent the learner or decision maker
2. Environment everything the agent interacts with and that responds to its actions
3. State $s_t$ a description of the situation at time $t$
4. Action $a_t$ a choice the agent makes at time $t$
5. Reward $r_t$ a numerical signal received after taking an action, indicating how good or bad the outcome was
6. Policy the agent's strategy for choosing an action given a state

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Discounted Return
content:
The return $G_t$ is the total reward the agent collects from time $t$ onward, with rewards further in the future counted for less using a discount factor $\gamma$ where $0 \le \gamma < 1$:
\[
G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}
\]

This is the same geometric-series idea used in compound interest, just applied to rewards shrinking into the future instead of money growing.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing Discounted Return
content:
Input: a sequence of rewards $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ received after time $t$, discount factor $\gamma$

Output: the discounted return $G_t$

1. Multiply the first reward $r_1$ by $\gamma^0=1$.
2. Multiply the second reward $r_2$ by $\gamma^1$.
3. Continue multiplying each subsequent reward $r_k$ by $\gamma^{k-1}$.
4. Sum all the discounted rewards to obtain $G_t$.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.7 --- Discounted Return with a High Discount Factor
content:
An agent receives rewards $4,3,2$ over three consecutive steps. Compute $G_0$ using $\gamma=0.9$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
G_0 &= 4 + (0.9)(3) + (0.9)^2(2) \\
&= 4 + 2.7 + (0.81)(2) \\
&= 4 + 2.7 + 1.62
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{G_0 = 8.32}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.8 --- Same Rewards with a Low Discount Factor
content:
Using the same rewards as Example 4.7 ($4,3,2$), compute $G_0$ using $\gamma=0.5$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
G_0 &= 4 + (0.5)(3) + (0.5)^2(2) \\
&= 4 + 1.5 + (0.25)(2) \\
&= 4 + 1.5 + 0.5
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{G_0 = 6}
Comparing Examples 4.7 and 4.8: the closer $\gamma$ is to $1$, the more the later rewards ($3$ and $2$) count toward the total; the closer $\gamma$ is to $0$, the more the agent behaves as if only the immediate reward mattered.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.9 --- Delayed Large Reward
content:
An agent receives rewards $-1,-1,10$ over three steps (two small penalties followed by a large reward). Compute $G_0$ using $\gamma=0.9$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
G_0 &= -1 + (0.9)(-1) + (0.9)^2(10) \\
&= -1 - 0.9 + (0.81)(10) \\
&= -1 - 0.9 + 8.1
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{G_0 = 6.2}
Even though the immediate reward is negative, the large discounted future reward makes the overall return positive — this is exactly why an RL agent must plan for delayed consequences rather than just the next single reward.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Reading the Discount Factor $$: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
Reading the Discount Factor $\gamma$:

1. $\gamma$ close to $0$: the agent is short-sighted and cares mainly about the immediate reward
2. $\gamma$ close to $1$: the agent is far-sighted and gives future rewards nearly as much weight as immediate ones
3. $\gamma$ must satisfy $0\le\gamma<1$ so that the infinite sum $G_t$ stays finite for an ongoing task

\subsection{Markov Chains}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Markov Chain
content: A Markov chain is a system that moves between a fixed set of states over time, where the transition to the next state depends only on probabilities attached to the current state. Every possible transition is described by a transition probability $P(s_{t+1}=j \mid s_t=i)$.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Markov Property
content:
The Markov property states that the future state depends only on the present state, not on the sequence of states that preceded it:
\[
P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, s_{t-1}, \ldots, s_1) = P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t)
\]
This is what makes the system "memoryless" beyond the current state.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Properties of a Transition Matrix
content:
1. Every transition probability satisfies $0 \le P(j\mid i) \le 1$ \hfill(valid probability)
2. The probabilities leaving any single state must sum to exactly $1$ \hfill(row sums to 1)
3. The probability of an entire path is the product of the transition probabilities along that path \hfill(chain rule under the Markov property)

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing the Probability of a State Sequence
content:
Input: a transition probability table, a known starting state, an ordered sequence of future states

Output: the probability of observing exactly that sequence of states

1. Start with probability $1$ at the given starting state.
2. For each step in the sequence, multiply the running probability by the transition probability from the current state to the next state in the sequence.
3. Move to the next state and repeat step 2 until the sequence ends.
4. Return the final product as the probability of the sequence.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.10 --- Probability of a Weather Sequence
content:
Using the transition probabilities in the diagram above (Sunny$\to$Sunny $0.8$, Sunny$\to$Rainy $0.2$, Rainy$\to$Rainy $0.6$, Rainy$\to$Sunny $0.4$), find the probability of the sequence Sunny, Sunny, Rainy given that day 1 is known to be Sunny.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Sunny},\text{Sunny},\text{Rainy}) &= P(S_1=\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny}\to\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny}\to\text{Rainy}) \\
&= 1 \times 0.8 \times 0.2
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P = 0.16}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.11 --- Probability of a Longer Sequence
content:
Using the same transition probabilities, find the probability of the sequence Rainy, Rainy, Sunny, Sunny given that day 1 is known to be Rainy.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Rainy},\text{Rainy},\text{Sunny},\text{Sunny}) &= 1 \times P(\text{Rainy}\to\text{Rainy}) \times P(\text{Rainy}\to\text{Sunny}) \times P(\text{Sunny}\to\text{Sunny}) \\
&= 1 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.8
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P = 0.192}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.12 --- Two-Step Transition Probability
content:
Using the same transition probabilities, find the probability that day 3 is Sunny given that day 1 is known to be Sunny (day 2 can be either state).

Solution:
Since day 2 is unknown, sum over both possibilities for day 2 (law of total probability):
$$\begin{align*}
P(S_3=\text{Sunny}\mid S_1=\text{Sunny}) &= P(S\to S)P(S\to S) + P(S\to R)P(R\to S) \\
&= (0.8)(0.8) + (0.2)(0.4) \\
&= 0.64 + 0.08
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P(S_3=\text{Sunny}\mid S_1=\text{Sunny}) = 0.72}
Notice the difference from Example 4.10: here the in-between state is not fixed, so every possible path to the destination must be added together, rather than following one single specified path.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Single-Path vs Marginal Probability: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] If
content:
Single-Path vs Marginal Probability:

1. If every intermediate state in the sequence is specified, simply multiply the transition probabilities along that one path (Examples 4.10, 4.11)
2. If an intermediate state is not specified, sum the products over every possible value it could take (Example 4.12)
3. This is the same "multiply along a branch, add across branches" rule used in probability trees

\subsection{Hidden Markov Models}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
content:
A Hidden Markov Model extends a Markov chain to situations where the true states are not directly observable. Instead, at each time step the hidden state probabilistically produces a visible observation. An HMM is defined by three components: the transition probabilities $A$ between hidden states, the emission probabilities $B$ of each hidden state producing each observation, and the initial probabilities $\pi$ of starting in each hidden state.

{\small Solid arrows: hidden state transitions ($A$). Dashed arrows: emission probabilities ($B$) to observations.}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing the Joint Probability of a Hidden State Path and an Observation Sequence
content:
Input: initial probabilities $\pi$, transition probabilities $A$, emission probabilities $B$, a specific hidden state sequence, an observation sequence of the same length

Output: the joint probability $P(\text{states, observations})$

1. Start with $\pi(\text{first state})$.
2. Multiply by the emission probability of the first observation given the first state.
3. For every following time step, multiply by the transition probability from the previous state to the current state, then multiply by the emission probability of the current observation given the current state.
4. Return the final product.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.13 --- Joint Probability for a Two-Step Path
content:
An HMM has $\pi(\text{Sunny})=0.6$, $\pi(\text{Rainy})=0.4$. Transitions: Sunny$\to$Sunny $0.7$, Sunny$\to$Rainy $0.3$, Rainy$\to$Rainy $0.6$, Rainy$\to$Sunny $0.4$. Emissions: $P(\text{Walk}\mid\text{Sunny})=0.6$, $P(\text{Shop}\mid\text{Sunny})=0.3$, $P(\text{Walk}\mid\text{Rainy})=0.1$, $P(\text{Shop}\mid\text{Rainy})=0.4$.
Compute $P(\text{states}=\text{Sunny},\text{Sunny};\ \text{obs}=\text{Walk},\text{Shop})$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P &= \pi(\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Walk}\mid\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny}\to\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Shop}\mid\text{Sunny}) \\
&= (0.6)(0.6) \times (0.7)(0.3) \\
&= 0.36 \times 0.21
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P = 0.0756}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.14 --- Joint Probability for a Different Path
content:
Using the same HMM as Example 4.13, compute $P(\text{states}=\text{Sunny},\text{Rainy};\ \text{obs}=\text{Walk},\text{Clean})$ where $P(\text{Clean}\mid\text{Rainy})=0.5$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P &= \pi(\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Walk}\mid\text{Sunny}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny}\to\text{Rainy}) \cdot P(\text{Clean}\mid\text{Rainy}) \\
&= (0.6)(0.6) \times (0.3)(0.5) \\
&= 0.36 \times 0.15
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P = 0.054}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Example 4.15 --- Joint Probability for a Three-Step Path
content:
Using the same HMM as Examples 4.13 and 4.14, compute \\
$P(\text{states}=\text{Rainy},\text{Rainy},\text{Sunny};\ \text{obs}=\text{Shop},\text{Clean},\text{Walk})$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P &= \pi(\text{Rainy}) \cdot P(\text{Shop}\mid\text{Rainy}) \cdot P(\text{Rainy}\to\text{Rainy}) \cdot P(\text{Clean}\mid\text{Rainy}) \cdot P(\text{Rainy}\to\text{Sunny})\\ \cdot P(\text{Walk}\mid\text{Sunny}) \\
&= (0.4)(0.4) \times (0.6)(0.5) \times (0.4)(0.6) \\
&= 0.16 \times 0.3 \times 0.24
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P = 0.01152}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Markov Chain vs Hidden Markov Model:
content:
Markov Chain vs Hidden Markov Model:
| \toprule Aspect | Markov Chain | Hidden Markov Model |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule States | Directly observed | Hidden (not observed) |
| What we see | The state sequence itself | Only an observation sequence |
| Parameters needed | Transition probabilities | Transition and emission probabilities |
| Typical question | Probability of a state path | Probability of an observation sequence |
| \bottomrule |  |  |

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Markov Decision Process (MDP)
content:
A Markov Decision Process formally models an RL environment using five components $(S,A,P,R,\gamma)$: a set of states $S$, a set of actions $A$, transition probabilities $P(s'\mid s,a)$ of reaching state $s'$ after taking action $a$ in state $s$, a reward function $R(s,a,s')$, and a discount factor $\gamma$. The Markov property (Section 4.2.2) applies here too: the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the full history.

This combines the Markov chain of Section 4.2.2 (states and transitions) with the actions and rewards of reinforcement learning (Section 4.2.1) into one formal framework.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Policy
content:
A policy $\pi$ is a rule that specifies which action the agent takes in each state, written $\pi(s)=a$ for a deterministic policy. Solving an MDP means finding the policy that maximizes the expected discounted return from every state.

\subsection{Value Functions and the Bellman Equation}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: State-Value Function
content:
The value $V^\pi(s)$ of a state $s$ under policy $\pi$ is the expected discounted return obtained by starting in $s$ and following $\pi$ thereafter. For a deterministic environment (each action leads to exactly one next state), it satisfies the Bellman equation:
\[
V^\pi(s) = R(s,\pi(s),s') + \gamma\, V^\pi(s')
\]
where $s'$ is the state reached from $s$ by taking action $\pi(s)$.

This is simply the discounted-return idea from Section 4.2.1 written recursively: the value of a state is this step's reward plus the (discounted) value of wherever you land next.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Properties of Value Functions
content:
1. A goal / terminal state has value $V(s)=0$, since no further reward is collected after reaching it \hfill(base case)
2. Values can be computed backward from the goal state toward earlier states \hfill(backward induction)
3. The optimal policy $\pi^\ast$ at each state chooses the action leading to the highest $R(s,a,s')+\gamma V(s')$ \hfill(greedy w.r.t.\ the value function)

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Computing State Values by Backward Induction (Deterministic MDP)
content:
Input: states, one deterministic transition and reward per action, discount factor $\gamma$, a known terminal state

Output: $V(s)$ for every state

1. Set $V(\text{terminal state}) = 0$.
2. Identify a state $s$ whose next state's value is already known.
3. Compute $V(s) = R(s,a,s') + \gamma V(s')$ for the action $a$ that will be taken from $s$.
4. Repeat steps 2 to 3, working backward, until every state has a computed value.
5. Return all computed values.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Example 4.22 --- Backward Value Computation on a Three-State Chain
content:
Using the diagram above ($S_1 \xrightarrow{a_1,r=-1} S_2 \xrightarrow{a_1,r=+10} S_3$, with $S_3$ terminal), compute $V(S_3)$, $V(S_2)$, and $V(S_1)$ using $\gamma=0.9$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
V(S_3) &= 0 \quad \text{(terminal state)} \\[4pt]
V(S_2) &= R(S_2,a_1,S_3) + \gamma V(S_3) = 10 + (0.9)(0) = 10 \\[4pt]
V(S_1) &= R(S_1,a_1,S_2) + \gamma V(S_2) = -1 + (0.9)(10) = -1+9
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{V(S_3)=0,\quad V(S_2)=10,\quad V(S_1)=8}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Example 4.23 --- Choosing Between Two Actions Using Values
content:
In state $S_1$ from Example 4.22, action $a_1$ leads to $S_2$ (reward $-1$) and action $a_2$ leads back to $S_1$ itself (reward $0$, i.e.\ staying put, so its "next value" is $V(S_1)$ again). Using $V(S_2)=10$ from Example 4.22 and $\gamma=0.9$, which action should the optimal policy choose at $S_1$: $a_1$ or $a_2$?

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Value of taking } a_1 &= R(S_1,a_1,S_2)+\gamma V(S_2) = -1+(0.9)(10) = 8 \\
\text{Value of taking } a_2 &= R(S_1,a_2,S_1)+\gamma V(S_1) = 0 + (0.9)(0) = 0 \quad (\text{using an initial guess } V(S_1)=0)
\end{align*}$$
Since $8 > 0$:
\boxed{\text{Optimal action at } S_1 \text{ is } a_1 \text{ (move toward the goal, not stay in place)}}
This matches the general rule from the theorembox: the optimal policy always picks the action with the higher $R(s,a,s')+\gamma V(s')$. ✓

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: MDP Summary — How Everything in
content:
MDP Summary — How Everything in This Chapter Connects:

1. The discounted return $G_t$ (Section 4.2.1) is what a value function $V(s)$ tries to predict in expectation from state $s$ onward
2. The Bellman equation rewrites that return recursively, one step at a time, instead of summing the whole future at once
3. Monte Carlo (Section 4.3) estimates $V(s)$ by averaging actual sampled returns; backward induction here computes $V(s)$ exactly when the model (transitions and rewards) is fully known
4. The exploration-exploitation trade-off (Section 4.4) arises precisely because an agent usually does not know $P$, $R$, or the true value function in advance, and must learn them through interaction
